list.listitem: The last naturally occurring case of smallpox was reported in 1977.C

Smallpox is characterized by several days of prodromal illness, followed by a diffuse macular rash beginning in the mouth and face and spreading centripetally, eventually covering the body with pedunculated pustules that scab and fall off over a period of about 2 weeks.C
Treatment has been supportive, with a mortality rate of approximately 30% for variola major.C
In animal models, antiviral drugs have been effective, but they have not been evaluated in humans.C
Tecovirimat (TPOXX) is approved for treatment of smallpox in persons weighing 13 kg or more.B

background.definition: Smallpox is an infectious disease caused by the variola virus.

list.listitem: The last naturally occurring case was reported in 1977 in Bangladesh. The disease has been eradicated through efforts of the CDC, although concerns remain that it could be used as a bioterror weapon.
Variola virus is stored in two maximum security laboratories in Russia and the USA. Despite the eradication of the disease unknown stocks may exist.
Variola virus
The variola virus is a dsDNA virus in the family Orthopoxvirus, which also includes vaccinia, cowpox, and monkeypox.
The virus reproduces in the cytoplasm of the infected cell, rather than the nucleus as with most other DNA viruses.
Variola only infects humans.
The incubation period for smallpox is 7 to 19 days, with an average of 10 to 14 days (https://www.cdc.gov/smallpox/index.html).

The smallpox vaccine is a live vaccine derived from vaccinia virus. The vaccine is administered using a bifurcated needle that is first dipped in the vaccine solution, followed by pricking the skin of the upper arm. The vaccine is no longer routinely administered, with its use generally limited to military personnel stationed overseas and laboratory workers who work with viral samples.C

Smallpox vaccination in pregnancy appears to be generally safe based on limited data, with no effect on the likelihood of spontaneous abortion, preterm birth, or stillbirth. A small increase in the risk of congenital malformation (2.4% vs 1.5%; RR 1.3; 95% CI 1.02-1.8) was seen for women vaccinated in the first trimester.B

In an outbreak, administration within 3 days of infection will likely reduce the severity of illness; vaccination within 4 to 7 days may provide some protection (https://www.cdc.gov/smallpox/index.html).
A modified vaccinia Ankara vaccine was evaluated in a randomized trial and found to provide similar immunogenicity but a smaller cutaneous reaction and fewer adverse events.
The United States maintains a strategic reserve of two antivirals (tecovirimat and brincidofovir), three different smallpox vaccines, and vaccinia immune globulin.

After a 10- to 14-day incubation period, smallpox causes several days of flu-like symptoms, followed by onset of a macular, erythematous rash that rapidly spreads and develops into pustules over a 3- to 7-day period.C
The pustules persist for 5 to 10 days, and then begin to scab and fall off, often leaving a depigmented scar.C

list.listitem: There are four types of smallpox: ○ Ordinary smallpox: the most common type in unvaccinated persons, with pustules filled with whitish fluid (tissue debris) appearing over the course of a week, slowly resolving and leaving scars. ○ Modified smallpox: less severe illness, occurring in those who have been previously vaccinated. ○ Malignant smallpox: a more severe form of the illness, often fatal, with a more severe prodrome and pustules that are more solid. ○ Hemorrhagic smallpox: severe form characterized by hemorrhage into the skin, GI tract, and mucous membranes.
Variola virus has a 10- to 14-day incubation period, during which the rash is not contagious.
Smallpox initially causes several days of flu-like symptoms, and patients may be contagious at this time.

This is followed by onset of a macular, erythematous rash, usually beginning in the mouth and on the tongue. Fever persists, and the rash then spreads to the face, arms, legs, and eventually hands, feet, and torso over a 24-hour period. Patients are highly contagious at this time, until all of the scabs have fallen off.

After 3 to 5 days, pustules filled with an opalescent thick fluid begin to appear all over the body. They eventually develop a dimple, giving the pustules their characteristic appearance. The macules may be confluent.
The pustules persist for 5 to 10 days, at which time they begin to form scabs and eventually fall off, often leaving a depigmented scar.
Once all of the scabs have fallen off, typically 3 weeks after onset, the person is no longer contagious (https://www.cdc.gov/smallpox/index.html).
Confirmatory tests include electron microscopy, Tzanck smear, direct fluorescent antibody testing, and increasingly real-time PCR.
A diagnostic algorithm has been developed based on major and minor criteria. See below and also .

Major criteria: (1) febrile prodrome with flu-like illness for 1 to 4 days prior to rash, (2) classic lesions (firm, round, well-circumscribed pustules that become dimpled or umbilicated), and (3) all lesions in a given part of the body are in the same stage of development.

Minor criteria: (1) centrifugal distribution, (2) lesions are initially oral, facial, and on forearms, (3) patient is toxic appearing, (4) evolution of lesions from macules to papules and pustules over 1 to 2 days, and (5) lesions occurring on palms and soles.
Patients with all three major criteria are high risk for smallpox; alert public health officials, isolate patient, and obtain diagnostic testing.

Patients with the first and either second or third major criteria are moderate risk, as are those with febrile prodrome and 4 or 5 of the minor criteria. Evaluate patients urgently by a specialist in ID or dermatology and test for varicella; if smallpox cannot be ruled out after evaluation, their risk is considered high.
Other patients are low risk for smallpox, with varicella the most likely diagnosis. Obtain testing for varicella and other conditions as indicated.
In animal models, antiviral therapy with tecovirimat, cidofovir, and brincidofovir has been effective. They have not been tested in human beings.C

Based on a study in primates with monkeypox, tecovirimat (PTOXX) was approved for treatment of human smallpox. For adults weighing 40 kg or more, the dose is 600 mg orally given twice daily for 14 days. For children, the dose is 200 mg twice daily for children weighing 13 kg to less than 25 kg, and 400 mg twice daily for children weighing 25 kg to less than 40 kg.B
CDC currently stockpiles both cidofovir and tecovirimat in the event of a bioterror event C (https://www.cdc.gov/smallpox/index.html).
The case-fatality rate is approximately 30% C (https://www.cdc.gov/smallpox/index.html).
Survivors often had extensive scars, and blindness was a possible complication C (https://www.cdc.gov/smallpox/index.html).
